direction: CLMUL-first prototype: build the minimal SIMD CSV lexer using PCLMULQDQ quote pairing as the core primitive
rationale: The CLMUL quote-pairing technique is the single most impactful innovation for CSV parsing because it eliminates the serial dependency that forces traditional parsers to process bytes sequentially. By building a working prototype around this primitive first, we establish the correctness of the approach on all RFC 4180 edge cases before optimizing further. The Sep parser (.NET) achieved 21 GB/s with a similar SIMD-first approach. The simdjson paper and the simdcsv Rust crate (friendlymatthew) demonstrate the viability of this exact technique for CSV.
first_step: Implement a Rust function that takes a &[u8] input and a previous carry bit, and returns: (comma_bitmask, newline_bitmask, in_string_bitmask, next_carry) for a 64-byte block. Use _mm_clmulepi64_si128 on x86 and vmull_p64 on ARM64. Write exhaustive tests covering: simple fields, quoted fields, embedded commas in quotes, embedded newlines in quotes, escaped quotes (double-quote), empty fields, trailing newlines, CRLF vs LF.
expected_signal: All RFC 4180 edge case tests pass. The function processes a 64-byte block in under 20 cycles on modern x86. The in_string_bitmask correctly masks all commas and newlines that appear within quoted regions.

direction: Two-phase architecture with Arrow output: build the full Phase 1 indexer + Phase 2 columnar extractor targeting Apache Arrow RecordBatch output
rationale: The two-phase architecture is the structural foundation that enables all other optimizations. By targeting Arrow output, we get zero-cost integration with the entire Arrow ecosystem (PyArrow/pandas, Polars, DataFusion, DuckDB). This is the approach that will yield the claimed 5x+ speedup over pandas — not just faster parsing, but also elimination of the row-to-column transposition that pandas' read_csv must perform internally. Arrow-csv (Rust) and Polars already use Arrow internally but their CSV readers don't use SIMD structural indexing, leaving a large performance gap.
first_step: Implement Phase 1: SIMD structural indexer that produces a Vec<u32> of field-boundary offsets and a Vec<u32> of row-boundary offsets. Implement Phase 2: a function that takes these indices + the input buffer and produces an arrow::RecordBatch with schema inferred from the first N rows (or provided). Benchmark end-to-end on a 1GB CSV (the NYC taxi dataset) against: pandas.read_csv, pyarrow.csv.read_csv, polars.read_csv, and xsv count.
expected_signal: Phase 1 runs at >5 GB/s on AVX2 hardware. End-to-end parsing (Phase 1 + Phase 2) is at least 3x faster than pyarrow.csv and 5x faster than pandas.read_csv on the taxi dataset. Memory usage is within 1.2x of the Arrow RecordBatch size (minimal overhead).

direction: Speculative parallelism: implement multi-threaded chunk-based parsing with speculative row synchronization for massive files
rationale: To reach maximum throughput on multi-core machines, we need to parallelize Phase 1 itself across multiple threads, each processing a separate region of the file. The challenge is that row boundaries depend on quote state, which is a serial dependency. The speculation approach — where each thread starts at a chunk boundary, scans forward to find a probable row start, and parses optimistically with later verification — is the key to breaking this serial dependency. This is analogous to how parallel lexers for programming languages handle string literals across chunk boundaries.
first_step: Divide a large input file into N chunks (one per thread). For each chunk except the first, scan the first ~1024 bytes to find a newline that is NOT inside a quoted region (heuristic: a newline followed by a character that is not a quote, or a newline preceded by an even number of quotes). Start Phase 1 from that synchronization point. After all threads complete, verify that chunk boundaries were correctly synchronized by checking that the last row of chunk K and first row of chunk K+1 are consistent.
expected_signal: Near-linear scaling from 1 to 8 threads on an 8-core machine for a 10GB CSV file. Synchronization overhead is <1% of total time. Mis-synchronization rate (where a thread starts mid-quoted-field) is <0.01% on real-world data and is always detected and corrected.

direction: Entropy-adaptive field extraction: profile columns and select extraction strategy based on field-width entropy
rationale: Real-world CSV files often have a mix of fixed-width columns (IDs, dates, zip codes) and variable-width columns (names, descriptions). By profiling the first 1024 rows, we can classify each column and apply the optimal extraction strategy. This is a novel contribution not present in any existing CSV parser — it bridges information theory with systems optimization. The FastLanes paper from VLDB 2023 demonstrated similar adaptive techniques for columnar encoding, achieving >100 billion integers/second via data-layout-aware processing.
first_step: Implement a profiler that collects field-width histograms for each column over the first 1024 rows. Compute Shannon entropy per column. Implement two extraction paths: (1) fixed-offset extraction for low-entropy columns (directly compute field offsets from predicted widths), (2) index-driven extraction for high-entropy columns (use Phase 1 structural index). Benchmark on a mixed CSV with 10 fixed-width columns and 10 variable-width columns.
expected_signal: Low-entropy columns (H < 0.5) achieve 2-3x faster extraction than the generic index-driven path. Overall parsing throughput on mixed files improves by 15-30% compared to uniform extraction. Entropy correctly predicts which columns benefit from the fixed-width fast path.
